title: The Break-Up

jokes.text: I'm gonna mount a TV on your wall. I just can't find a stud. So you made nine holes in my wall? No, those are for the shelves, dummy.
jokes.setup: Dennis says he can't find a stud in the wall to mount a TV.
jokes.punchline: He's made nine holes — but insists those are for shelves, as if that's a completely separate and acceptable project.
jokes.explanation: Solid cold-open joke establishing Dennis as an oblivious, destructive boyfriend. The logic that the nine holes are 'for the shelves' and therefore don't count is wonderfully idiotic. Character-specific: only Dennis would partition his chaos into separate categories and act like that's fine.

jokes.text: It's gonna be like a hospital.
jokes.setup: Dennis is excitedly pitching wall-mounted TV as a home improvement.
jokes.punchline: His highest aspiration for Liz's apartment is that it resemble a hospital room.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical character joke — Dennis's idea of aspirational living is a hospital room. It's funny precisely because he says it with genuine enthusiasm. One line that tells you everything about him.

jokes.text: I don't want a shelf... Whose horse is that?
jokes.setup: Liz is mid-complaint about Dennis's home renovation disaster.
jokes.punchline: She is interrupted mid-sentence by noticing what is apparently a large dog (Great Dane) that she mistakes for a horse, undercutting her grievance completely.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully timed visual-gag-meets-misdirection. The comedic value is in the abrupt, mid-sentence pivot from domestic grievance to bewilderment at what she's seeing. The 'horse' misidentification is funny and economical — it's a Great Dane, but her confusion sells the absurdity of the situation Dennis has created.

jokes.text: Now, why is it important to tell me that the muggers were black? / They weren't muggers. They were cops. / So why don't you just say he was running from some cops? / I don't know, I mean, you're a racist for assuming that they weren't cops.
jokes.setup: Liz challenges Dennis for racially specifying the men chasing his cousin.
jokes.punchline: Dennis reveals they were cops, turning Liz's moral correction back on her — she assumed 'black guys with guns' meant muggers, not cops.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural joke. Dennis sets up what seems like casual racism, Liz (and the audience) prepares to call it out, then the rug pull: they were cops, making Liz's assumption the reveal. Then Dennis lands the punchline by calling her racist — which is both absurd and logically coherent in the most infuriating way. Multi-layered, character-specific to Dennis's idiotic-but-occasionally-accidentally-correct worldview.

jokes.text: Ack, allergies are all mental.
jokes.setup: Liz notes she's allergic to dogs and can't have one in the apartment.
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses allergies as entirely psychosomatic with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: Quick, punchy character-establishment line. Dennis as an anti-intellectual blowhard who confidently dismisses medical science. It gets a small laugh and sets up a callback later. Economy is its strength.

jokes.text: You can't kick me out. I love you! / You can't kick me out. I got squatter's rights. / Which is it: you love me or you got squatter's rights? / I don't see why they're mutually exclusive!
jokes.setup: Dennis tries two different arguments for why Liz can't kick him out — love, then legal rights.
jokes.punchline: When challenged on the contradiction, he insists both can coexist — love and squatter's rights are, to him, perfectly compatible.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke that captures Dennis's character in miniature. The pivot from romantic plea to legal threat is funny enough; the insistence that they're 'not mutually exclusive' is the genuine laugh. It's quotable, character-specific, and structurally tight — the escalation lands because both arguments are equally ridiculous coming from him.

jokes.text: He's a comple loser. / Oh, Jenna, don't say that. You know, he had some good moments. / Hi. I got donuts. / What's up, brown eyes? I made chili. / (next scene) Hey... You wanna... wanna order cheese steaks?
jokes.setup: Liz defends Dennis by saying he had 'some good moments.'
jokes.punchline: Three cutaway flashbacks of Dennis's 'good moments' are all food-related — donuts, chili, cheese steaks — nothing emotional or meaningful.
jokes.explanation: A tight cutaway gag in the 30 Rock style. The joke is in the cumulative bathos: each 'good moment' reduces to Dennis holding food. 'I guess they were mostly food related' is the button that earns the laugh by acknowledging the joke. The structure (three beats + button) is textbook.

jokes.text: I guess they were mostly food related.
jokes.setup: Three flashback 'good moments' of Dennis have all been him arriving with food.
jokes.punchline: Liz's resigned, understated summary acknowledges the obvious while saving face.
jokes.explanation: The button to the cutaway gag. Economical and self-aware without being meta. Liz's deadpan acceptance of how low the bar has been is both funny and character-revealing.

jokes.text: Oh, you mean like at a discotheque?
jokes.setup: Jenna suggests they go out to meet new people after the breakup.
jokes.punchline: Liz, socially out of touch, calls it a 'discotheque' — a word that hasn't been in common use since 1979.
jokes.explanation: A quick character joke revealing Liz's social awkwardness and datedness. The word 'discotheque' is doing all the work — it's period-wrong in a way that's perfectly calibrated to her character. Jenna's 'Oh, boy' is the straight-man button.

jokes.text: Allergies are all in the mind, Lemon. I used to have a wicked peanut allergy. And now, witness.
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses Liz's allergies. He claims to have cured his own peanut allergy through force of will — 'witness.'
jokes.punchline: The implied visual gag: Jack is about to demonstrate by eating a peanut. The callback to Dennis's identical line ('allergies are all mental') recontextualizes it as shared male obliviousness. 'Witness' is the grandiose button.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback that earns more on second viewing. The show has now made the same idiotic claim through both Dennis and Jack — a blue-collar buffoon and a corporate executive — suggesting it's a universal male delusion. Jack saying 'witness' with supreme confidence before presumably eating a peanut is peak Jack Donaghy character comedy.

jokes.text: Let's just say she's a high-ranking African-American member of the Bush administration. / Are you dating Condoleeza Rice?
jokes.setup: Jack cryptically describes his mystery girlfriend with a very narrow description.
jokes.punchline: The description is so specific that it points to exactly one person, which Liz immediately names.
jokes.explanation: Classic setup where the 'mystery' is transparently obvious, making the punchline about Liz's (and the audience's) immediate recognition. The specificity of 'high-ranking African-American member of the Bush administration' is funny because Jack thinks it's vague. Good economy.

jokes.text: Yeah, and it must be hard for her to get cell phone reception when she's so far up the president's butt.
jokes.setup: Jack mentions his girlfriend (implied Condoleeza Rice) travels a lot and it's hard to connect.
jokes.punchline: Liz subverts the complaint about phone reception with a political jab about Condi's proximity to Bush.
jokes.explanation: Sharp political one-liner that works on two levels — literal cell reception and political sycophancy. Characteristic of Liz's liberal politics clashing with Jack's world. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I'm choosing to ignore that remark on the basis that you are a godless, glassy-eyed Clintonista.
jokes.setup: Liz has made a political jab at Bush/Rice.
jokes.punchline: Jack's dismissal is so specifically political and loaded ('godless, glassy-eyed Clintonista') that it's a joke about his character more than a real rebuttal.
jokes.explanation: 'Glassy-eyed Clintonista' is a great coinage — specific, insulting, and revealing of Jack's political identity. The word 'Clintonista' alone earns the laugh. High character integration — this is pure Jack.

jokes.text: Jack shows Liz two gifts: an attaché case vs. 'this collection of ladies' unmentionables with snaps and openings all over the place'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz whether to give his girlfriend something dignified or something sexual.
jokes.punchline: The description of the lingerie as having 'snaps and openings all over the place' is both clinical and graphic — Jack describing sexy lingerie with the detached language of a hardware catalog.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Jack's characteristically businesslike language applied to something intimate. 'Snaps and openings all over the place' is funny because of how anatomically bureaucratic it sounds. Good character integration — only Jack talks about lingerie like it's an equipment manifest.

jokes.text: Liz screams 'Attaché!' in response to Jack's gift options
jokes.setup: Jack presents two wildly different gift options for Condoleezza Rice
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate, emphatic single-word answer — clearly horrified by the lingerie option — is a pure reaction beat
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word captures Liz's entire reaction. The joke is in the immediacy and emphasis. Not particularly original but executed perfectly.

jokes.text: Yeah, it's pretty good. But I think the boobs should swing more. Yeah, then I could go: 'Rodney, don't make me come over there and beat you in the head with one of my boom-booms!'
jokes.setup: Tracy is apparently watching/workshopping a female character (Shamanda) in drag on the show.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's note about the performance is that the fake breasts should swing more, so he can use them as weapons while delivering an absurd threat.
jokes.explanation: Tracy at his most Tracy — the note about boob-swinging physics leading to 'beat you in the head with one of my boom-booms' is absurdist gold. The line 'boom-booms' becomes a running gag. Only Tracy Jordan would give this as a serious performance note, and the specificity of 'Rodney' makes it feel like a real beef. High quotability.

jokes.text: What? Everybody loves a dude in a dress. I mean, those are the best Bugs Bunnies.
jokes.setup: Someone raises concerns about a Black comedian doing drag being demeaning.
jokes.punchline: Frank's counterargument is that 'those are the best Bugs Bunnies' — reducing the entire cultural debate to cartoon cross-dressing.
jokes.explanation: Frank's cultural analysis bottoms out at Bugs Bunny in drag, which is a characteristically lowbrow punchline from him. The appeal to Bugs Bunny as the definitive authority is funny. Not exceptional but functional.

jokes.text: Frank, there are large pockets of African-American culture that Caucasians know nothing about. The stigma of drag is one of them.
jokes.setup: Frank defends drag using Bugs Bunny
jokes.punchline: Toofer delivers this cultural education with the weary condescension of a man who has explained things to white people his entire life
jokes.explanation: Toofer's role as the hyper-educated, hyper-conscious Black intellectual is on full display. The comedy is in his earnestness — he genuinely believes this, and he's not entirely wrong, which makes him sympathetic and funny simultaneously.

jokes.text: Hunky Grandma Be Trippin' made $96 million.
jokes.setup: Frank claims he's played a woman before to support his argument that drag is universally loved.
jokes.punchline: The invented movie title 'Hunky Grandma Be Trippin'' is a pitch-perfect parody of a certain strain of broad Black comedy films, made funnier by coming from a white Italian-American writer.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding fake movie title. 'Hunky Grandma Be Trippin'' is one of those rare constructed jokes where the name itself is the entire joke — it parodies a specific subgenre (Tyler Perry/Big Momma's House-adjacent) with perfect economy. The $96 million box office figure adds a layer of absurd specificity. High originality.

jokes.text: We never would have stooped so low on Black Frasier.
jokes.setup: Toofer argues that drag demeans Black comedians by citing a show called 'Black Frasier.'
jokes.punchline: The existence of 'Black Frasier' is itself the joke — a show that is apparently exactly what it sounds like.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'Black Frasier' is one of the great fake TV show names in 30 Rock history — the simplicity of just adding 'Black' to an existing highbrow show is absurdly funny. Toofer citing it as a standard of dignity makes it even better. Perfect character integration: Toofer is exactly the Harvard-educated Black man who would both have been on Black Frasier and consider it prestigious.

jokes.text: Black Frasier scene: 'Niles, this Beaujolais is impeccable. It's both fruity and precocious.' / 'That's not the only thing around here that's fruity and precocious.'
jokes.setup: Toofer describes/acts out a scene from 'Black Frasier' to prove the show's quality.
jokes.punchline: The shown scene is entirely faithful to actual Frasier — pretentious wine talk and a Niles-style gay joke — but performed/written exactly as Frasier would be, just with Black characters. The joke is that it's indistinguishable from the real show.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly executed extension of the Black Frasier joke. The dialogue is spot-on Frasier pastiche (Beaujolais, 'fruity and precocious' as double entendre), making the bit funny on two levels: it parodies Frasier and validates Toofer's genuine snobbery. The fact that this IS good Frasier material deepens the comedy.

jokes.text: What? It was huge on BET. Every Thursday night at about 9:00 or 9:15.
jokes.setup: Frank expresses disbelief that Black Frasier existed.
jokes.punchline: Toofer defends it by giving suspiciously vague timeslot information ('9:00 or 9:15') — the uncertainty undercuts the confidence and implies the show may have had scheduling issues, or perhaps never existed as advertised.
jokes.explanation: The hedging of '9:00 or 9:15' is a small but precise comedic detail — Toofer is certain the show was prestigious but fuzzy on the facts. It suggests either low viewership or that the show was frequently pre-empted, both of which are quietly funny.

jokes.text: Think about it, Tracy. All the best African-American comedians refuse to do drag. Chris Rock doesn't do it. Dr. Cosby doesn't do it. Bernie Mac doesn't do it 'cause he'd be ugly as hell.
jokes.setup: Toofer makes a principled argument that great Black comedians don't do drag.
jokes.punchline: The list of principled objectors ends with Bernie Mac's exception — not principle, but aesthetics ('he'd be ugly as hell').
jokes.explanation: Classic list joke with a rule-breaking final entry. The first two items establish a dignified principle; the third (Bernie Mac) shatters it with a completely different — and meaner — logic. Well-constructed, well-executed. The specificity of the three names grounds it.

jokes.text: I'll do it. I mean, my parents raised me as a girl for, like, ten years.
jokes.setup: The writers need someone to wear the Shamanda dress after Tracy refuses.
jokes.punchline: Pete volunteers, revealing a deeply dark detail about his childhood completely matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Pete's casual revelation that his parents raised him as a girl for ten years — delivered as if it's a reasonable qualification — is darkly funny and perfectly timed. The 'like, ten years' hedge makes it worse. The beat that follows ('What? I told you guys that.') deepens it. Classic 30 Rock dark backstory drop.

jokes.text: What? I told you guys that. (beat of silence/disbelief from everyone)
jokes.setup: Pete reveals his parents raised him as a girl for ten years.
jokes.punchline: Everyone's apparent horrified silence, met by Pete's genuine confusion that this is new information — he thought he'd mentioned it.
jokes.explanation: The button to the Pete joke, and arguably funnier than the setup. The idea that he mentioned this before — that this is common knowledge among his coworkers — recontextualizes the entire writers' room relationship. Perfect sitcom deadpan beat.

jokes.text: I know this great karaoke place where you can get a pedicure while you sing.
jokes.setup: Jenna promises no more karaoke after their last embarrassing duet.
jokes.punchline: She then immediately suggests a karaoke place — just one with simultaneous foot care, as if that changes everything.
jokes.explanation: Decent character joke about Jenna's obliviousness — she promises no karaoke then suggests karaoke. The pedicure addition is a nice absurdist touch but the joke is fairly predictable.

jokes.text: Liz and Jenna's previous karaoke duet: 'When I'm right here, you need to be here. Not here. Here is embarrassing.'
jokes.setup: Liz protests no more karaoke after their last duet.
jokes.punchline: The flashback shows Liz and Jenna apparently arguing about stage positioning DURING a karaoke performance, breaking down into a spatial dispute mid-song — visible from the dialogue which only makes sense as a choreography argument.
jokes.explanation: Inferred visual gag — the dialogue only makes sense if they're arguing about stage positions during performance ('When I'm right here, you need to be here. Here is embarrassing'). The fact that the karaoke performance collapsed into a staging argument is characteristically Liz/Jenna.

jokes.text: Check this out. I think Jack is dating Condi Rice. / Oh, God, that's huge!
jokes.setup: Liz mentions the Condi Rice rumor to a coworker.
jokes.punchline: The reaction 'Oh, God, that's huge!' treats this as celebrity gossip rather than a geopolitical concern.
jokes.explanation: Functional callback joke — the Condi Rice rumor being treated as celebrity gossip is a mild laugh. Not sophisticated but it moves the story.

jokes.text: Dude, that Shamanda character was the best thing of the night. What was her line? Say it again. / Rodney! Don't make me come over there and beat on you with my boom-booms!
jokes.setup: The Shamanda sketch has aired and was a hit.
jokes.punchline: Frank begs Tracy to repeat the 'boom-booms' line, which Tracy delivers again with full commitment.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the 'boom-booms' bit gets extra mileage from Tracy's commitment on the repeat. The line is already quotable from its first appearance; hearing it again with full energy confirms its status as the episode's breakout gag.

jokes.text: Whoopi Goldberg does it every day!
jokes.setup: Frank is listing Black comedians who do drag (Eddie Murphy, Martin Lawrence, Jamie Foxx, Flip Wilson).
jokes.punchline: He adds Whoopi Goldberg to the list — implying she presents as masculine in her daily life. Mean-spirited but committed.
jokes.explanation: Borderline cheap shot but delivered with enough commitment and speed that it works in context. The logic of the list (male comedians who've done drag) makes Whoopi's inclusion a surprise subversion. Not high art but gets a laugh.

jokes.text: You stole a franchise from me! Shamanda could have been a movie!
jokes.setup: Tracy had refused to do the Shamanda drag sketch; someone else did it and it was a hit.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's outrage that he was talked out of his own franchise opportunity — after being the one who refused — is peak Tracy logic.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's completely unself-aware outrage at losing a franchise HE gave up is a great character comedy beat. 'Shamanda could have been a movie' delivered with genuine grief is funny because it's both absurd and weirdly plausible in a Hollywood context.

jokes.text: Our comedy gotta do more than make people laugh. Gotta make people think. I wanna hold a mirror up to society, and then win world record for biggest mirror.
jokes.setup: Tracy declares his artistic vision for socially conscious comedy.
jokes.punchline: His articulate-sounding artistic statement derails into a literal world record ambition for the size of the mirror.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes and a contender for the series' best Tracy lines. The setup uses the classic comedy trope ('hold a mirror up to society') and then makes it literal with the Guinness-level ambition of winning the record for the biggest mirror. It's funny because (a) it sounds like something Tracy would genuinely pursue, (b) the escalation is perfectly timed, and (c) it captures his character's collision of genuine artistic ambition and complete lunacy. Near-anthology quality.

jokes.text: You and Jenna play Sleestaks from Land of the Lost and you're trying to get a small business loan. Because you want to open up a pancake house called Slee's Stacks.
jokes.setup: Liz pitches a sketch to Tracy about race relations.
jokes.punchline: The sketch has nothing to do with race — it's about reptilian monsters from a '70s kids show trying to get a business loan, with a pun restaurant name.
jokes.explanation: 'Slee's Stacks' is a beautifully terrible pun — the kind of name that only makes sense if you're a white TV writer who thinks they're being clever. The sketch premise is so spectacularly off-base as a response to Tracy's request for race-conscious material that it perfectly illustrates Liz's cultural blind spot. Strong originality.

jokes.text: Are you black?
jokes.setup: Liz has pitched Sleestak sketch as meaningful race-relations comedy.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's single-sentence verdict on Liz's cultural competence — three words that say everything.
jokes.explanation: Perfect three-word punchline. Tracy's deadpan question after Liz's absurd pitch is one of the episode's best jokes — perfectly economical, deeply character-appropriate (Tracy recognizing the cultural miss), and funny as a pure reaction beat. The ten-second pause before this response (implied by the scene marker gap at 07:09-07:19) amplifies the comedy.

jokes.text: Are you black? (Tracy's response to Liz's Sleestak pitch, followed by a long pause)
jokes.setup: Liz has just delivered her Sleestak pitch as an attempt to write something for a Black comedian
jokes.punchline: Tracy's only response is to question whether Liz is Black — the simplest possible expression of disbelief at how culturally off-base the pitch was
jokes.explanation: Three words followed by a beat of silence. Maximum economy, maximum impact. The question is rhetorical — of course Liz is not Black — but asking it is the perfect encapsulation of how far off-target she is. The pause after makes it land even harder. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.text: I know what I know. Next time I see Putin, I'm gonna kick his teeth in.
jokes.setup: Jack suspects his girlfriend (Condi) is cheating — another man in the picture.
jokes.punchline: The 'other man' is Vladimir Putin, and Jack's response to romantic rivalry is to threaten to assault a world leader.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The geopolitical absurdity — Jack Donaghy jealous of Putin, threatening to 'kick his teeth in' as if settling a bar fight with a world leader — is perfectly in character. Jack's alpha-male posturing at a global scale is one of the show's best recurring comic ideas, and this is a crystalline example. High originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Izzle. 'A suffix that can be used to take the place of anything.' / Well, now you're just being patronizzle.
jokes.setup: Liz and Toofer are apparently in an argument about African-American vernacular, and Liz reads a definition of '-izzle.'
jokes.punchline: Toofer uses '-izzle' himself to call out Liz's condescension — 'patronizzle' — which simultaneously proves the suffix works and demonstrates his own code-switching fluency.
jokes.explanation: Clever wordplay joke — 'patronizzle' is a great coinage that works both as a pun and as a piece of characterization (Toofer deploying the slang he was defending to shut down Liz's attempt to explain it to him). The joke earns its cleverness.

jokes.text: You know who would love this argument? My racist grandfather.
jokes.setup: Liz and Toofer are fighting about language and cultural ownership.
jokes.punchline: Liz's non-sequitur self-deprecation — her racist grandfather would enjoy watching two people fight about this — is darkly funny and deflates the argument.
jokes.explanation: A self-aware joke about the absurdity of the debate from Liz's perspective. Admitting her racist grandfather would enjoy the argument is a disarmingly honest piece of character self-awareness. Decent.

jokes.text: I thought writing with you was gonna be like two brothers writing together. / We're not even speaking the same language. / That's right. I'm speaking English.
jokes.setup: Tracy complains he and Liz aren't connecting on writing — 'not speaking the same language.'
jokes.punchline: Toofer's retort: 'That's right. I'm speaking English.' — pointing out that Tracy's speech patterns are themselves a language barrier.
jokes.explanation: Sharp comeback that works on two levels — Toofer is both being snobbish and making a legitimate linguistic observation. The 'two brothers' setup primes us for racial commentary, but the punchline pivots to class and education. Good character integration for Toofer.

jokes.text: Standing there with your pants that fit. Using a wallet. Drinking Starbucks.
jokes.setup: Tracy accuses Toofer of abandoning his cultural heritage.
jokes.punchline: The specific grievances — pants that fit, owning a wallet, drinking Starbucks — are a hilariously specific list of 'sellout' markers.
jokes.explanation: A strong list joke where each item is deliberately more mundane than the last. 'Pants that fit' is unexpectedly funny as a cultural marker, and 'using a wallet' is perfectly deadpan. The specificity is Tracy's voice at its best.

jokes.text: That's my Harvard a cappella group the Crocodillos. I had a solo in Like A Prayer.
jokes.setup: Tracy accuses Toofer of abandoning Black heritage; Toofer shows evidence of his background.
jokes.punchline: His evidence of Black cultural credibility is... being in a Harvard a cappella group called the Crocodillos and having a solo in a Madonna song.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character joke. The Crocodillos is a perfect Harvard a cappella group name, and the detail that Toofer's cultural heritage defense is a solo in a Madonna song is both absurd and devastatingly on-point. It proves Tracy's argument while Toofer thinks it refutes it. Near-perfect character integration — this is ONLY funny because it's Toofer.

jokes.text: Yeah, I think they're from the firm of Date-Rape, Coke-ington Cheeseball, and Jag.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if the attractive men at the bar are Wall Street guys.
jokes.punchline: Jenna gives them a law firm name that itemizes every worst-case scenario they represent: date rape, cocaine, being a cheeseball, and being a jag(off).
jokes.explanation: Instant-classic 30 Rock one-liner. 'Date-Rape, Coke-ington Cheeseball, and Jag' is a perfectly constructed fake law firm name that escalates from specific crime to drug to insults. 'Coke-ington' as a portmanteau surname is particularly inspired. High quotability and originality.

jokes.text: Oh, really, dude? I gotta move my coat? There's like four empty seats down there. Can't you just be cool?
jokes.setup: A man approaches to ask if the seat next to Liz is taken.
jokes.punchline: Liz responds with aggressive irritation to what is clearly a flirting approach, completely failing to read the social situation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon character moment — her instinct is to defend her coat like territory rather than recognize an approach. 'Can't you just be cool?' to someone trying to flirt with her is beautifully oblivious. High character integration.

jokes.text: That guy wanted to buy you a drink. / Really? I already have a drink. / Do you think he'd buy me mozzarella sticks?
jokes.setup: Jenna points out Liz just drove away a man who wanted to buy her a drink.
jokes.punchline: Liz's response pivots immediately from 'I have a drink' to calculating whether she could parlay the social situation into mozzarella sticks.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Liz Lemon joke. The pivot from romantic opportunity to appetizer procurement is a great character beat — Liz's romantic disengagement and food fixation expressed in one line. 'Do you think he'd buy me mozzarella sticks?' is instantly quotable and perfect character comedy. Callbacks to her food-centric perspective established with Dennis.

jokes.text: Oh, he knows where Bin Laden is, come on! The Carlyle Group. The Unocal Pipeline. The assassination of Olof Palme.
jokes.setup: Liz is apparently talking to/near a man she's attracted to, but her conversation turns political.
jokes.punchline: Liz's attempt at bar conversation spirals into a breathless conspiracy theory download — Bin Laden, the Carlyle Group, the assassination of a Swedish Prime Minister — completely torpedoing any romantic possibility.
jokes.explanation: The inclusion of the Olof Palme assassination is the joke's escalation peak — it's such a deep cut conspiracy theory reference that it signals Liz has completely lost the room. The increasingly obscure references function as a character portrait: this is how Liz Lemon wrecks a date.

jokes.text: You could put a long, blonde wig on a ferret and it would look like Jessica Simpson.
jokes.setup: Someone says an attractive woman at the bar looks like Jessica Simpson.
jokes.punchline: Liz dismisses Jessica Simpson's looks by saying any ferret in a wig could achieve the same effect.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed celebrity jab. The 'ferret in a wig' image is specific and funny enough to rise above generic celebrity insult. The visual is memorably absurd. Slightly cheap but executed well.

jokes.text: And by the way, Jessica Simpson would think that you are old and gross. So good luck with that.
jokes.setup: Liz has just insulted Jessica Simpson.
jokes.punchline: She then defends Simpson by pointing out that Simpson would find the man in question — who apparently made the comparison — old and gross. Liz ends up accidentally defending the person she just insulted.
jokes.explanation: The flip — Liz going from 'Simpson looks like a ferret' to 'Simpson's standards are higher than yours' — is a nice bit of comic logic. Not exceptional but extends the joke well.

jokes.text: Also, you have really pretty eyes. Oh, hi. (song begins) I learned the truth at seventeen. That love was meant for beauty queens.
jokes.setup: Liz has apparently started connecting with a man who compliments her eyes.
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts to/reveals she has somehow initiated a karaoke performance of 'At Seventeen' (a song about being too ugly to date in high school) — possibly after requesting or being pulled into it — an exquisitely embarrassing song choice for a woman trying to attract someone.
jokes.explanation: Excellent sequence. The choice of 'At Seventeen' by Janis Ian — a song specifically about being too plain and overlooked for love — is inspired. It's perfectly wrong for the situation and serves as an unintentional public declaration of Liz's insecurities. The structural cut from flirting to this song is the joke. High character integration.

jokes.text: Hey, you're bumming us out.
jokes.setup: Liz is performing 'At Seventeen' — a melancholy song about adolescent rejection — at a bar.
jokes.punchline: The bar audience's complaint is not about the singing quality but the emotional content: it's too sad.
jokes.explanation: Good button to the karaoke bit. The complaint is about emotional content rather than talent, which is a funnier criticism — she's not bad, she's just unbearably sad.

jokes.text: I thought bars were open till 4:00. / Nope, 11:30. Let's get you to bed.
jokes.setup: The girls' night has apparently ended early and badly.
jokes.punchline: The bar closed at 11:30 — they didn't stay late; the bar literally closed around them. Jenna treats Liz like a tired child ('Let's get you to bed').
jokes.explanation: Quiet but effective scene-closer. The 11:30 bar close is a sad indictment of how the evening went. 'Let's get you to bed' from Jenna is a nice maternal role reversal. Functional.

jokes.text: Mr. Jordan called me... the N-word. / And? / And I was really offended. / Because... / Because it's a racial slur. / Brothers talk to other brothers like that. I was being friendly.
jokes.setup: Toofer has filed a harassment complaint about Tracy using the N-word.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's defense — 'I was being friendly' — frames a racial slur as a term of endearment, which is both his genuine belief and an absurd position in an HR meeting.
jokes.explanation: The HR meeting framing makes a nuanced cultural discussion into a cringe comedy sequence. Tracy's sincere 'I was being friendly' and the HR rep's leading questions ('And?', 'Because...') create a funny procedural rhythm for an uncomfortable topic.

jokes.text: Yes, Toofer. You see, in the last decade or so, the African-American community has re-appropriated that word as a way of depriving it of its meaning.
jokes.setup: Tracy is trying to explain to Toofer why it was okay to use the N-word on him
jokes.punchline: Tracy delivers a perfectly articulate, academically correct explanation of linguistic re-appropriation — completely at odds with his usual manner of speaking, and also somewhat undermining his own earlier characterization of Liz as out of touch
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Tracy suddenly becoming eloquent and academically correct — the contrast with his usual register is the joke. He's explaining the scholarship of the slur while being the exact person who wielded it.

jokes.text: It's okay for us to use it with each other. You can call me that. It's a term of endearment.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains to the HR rep that the word is fine between Black people.
jokes.punchline: He invites the (presumably white or ambiguous) HR rep to use it, expanding the permission beyond the intended context.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation in the HR meeting — Tracy keeps expanding the permission structure beyond what the moment calls for. Inviting the HR rep to use the word is both characteristically generous and completely chaotic.

jokes.text: I want you to be my brother, my homeboy, my n-- [Toofer cuts him off]
jokes.setup: Tracy attempts to extend the olive branch to Toofer using the same fraternal language from before.
jokes.punchline: Toofer cuts him off before completion — the running gag of the word being cut off escalates here with maximum cringe.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Tracy attempting to use the word and getting cut off is well-executed. Each iteration adds a layer — the first was friendly, the second was in HR, now it's an attempted reconciliation. The escalating contexts make each cut-off funnier.

jokes.text: Whoa! This meeting is adjourned. / No cool, homie! / You might as well spread me down with a fire hose. / Just sounds so hateful coming from you! Ugh! I wish to file a complaint.
jokes.setup: Tracy says the word in the HR meeting trying to bond with Toofer.
jokes.punchline: The HR rep shuts the meeting down; Toofer files a counter-complaint; the fire hose reference escalates to civil rights imagery; chaos ensues.
jokes.explanation: The 'fire hose' reference (civil rights imagery applied to being offended in an office) is an unexpectedly dark escalation. The simultaneous complaint filings and Tracy's 'No cool, homie' are good chaos. The scene resolves the HR plot with appropriate absurdist energy.

jokes.text: Dennis's letter: 'While other women have bigger boobs than you, no woman has as big a heart.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has written Liz a goodbye letter.
jokes.punchline: His attempt at a romantic compliment begins by noting other women have bigger breasts than Liz — the kind of backhanded romantic opening that only Dennis would think was touching.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The letter structure is perfect for sustained cringe comedy, and the opener — acknowledging other women's superior chest size as his first clause in a love letter — is a masterpiece of oblivious backhanded complimenting. Only Dennis Duffy would write this and mean it as romantic. Extremely high character integration and originality.

jokes.text: And for the first time since the '86 World Series, I cried. I cried like a big dumb homo.
jokes.setup: Dennis's letter describes his emotional response to seeing Liz going out.
jokes.punchline: His crying is calibrated against the 1986 World Series (i.e., very rarely/significantly), then undercut by the phrase 'big dumb homo' — simultaneously self-deprecating and homophobic.
jokes.explanation: The '86 World Series benchmark for emotional frequency is great New York-specific character work (the Mets). 'Big dumb homo' is exactly the self-deprecating language Dennis would use when trying to express genuine emotion — he reaches for vulnerability and lands on a slur. Darkly funny because it's real.

jokes.text: And if it was up to me, we would be together forever. But there's a new thing called 'women's liberation' which gives you women the right to choose, and you have chosen to abort me.
jokes.setup: Dennis acknowledges the relationship is over.
jokes.punchline: His framing of women's liberation as a 'new thing' and his use of 'abort' as a metaphor for being broken up with — combining reproductive rights language with his romantic rejection — is spectacularly wrong-headed.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of the strongest in the series. 'Women's liberation' as a 'new thing' (it's the 2000s), combined with 'you have chosen to abort me' — applying pro-choice language to a breakup — is an extraordinary piece of writing. It perfectly captures Dennis's oblivious misogyny, his pseudo-acknowledgment of women's rights, and his complete misapplication of political language. The line is quotable, original, character-specific, and earned. This is anchor-quality comedy: comparable to the Snip Snap benchmark.

jokes.text: The guy just came in here and bared his soul to you. What are you, made of stone? / Am I crazy? The guy's a disaster, right?
jokes.setup: After Dennis delivers his letter and leaves, Pete seems moved by it.
jokes.punchline: Pete's genuine emotional response to Dennis's disaster letter — 'what are you, made of stone?' — implies the letter worked on him, while Liz maintains appropriate perspective.
jokes.explanation: Decent reaction comedy — Pete's emotional reaction to Dennis's letter reveals something unexpected about Pete (or just his loneliness). Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Hey. Threesome? How about it, huh? Mmm! I'm just saying... after last night... maybe he's not such a bad choice.
jokes.setup: Pete (and the show) suggests Dennis might not be a bad choice for Liz after his emotional letter.
jokes.punchline: Dennis appears and his first words are an invitation to a threesome — completely undercutting the letter's sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Good comedic undercut — Dennis's heartfelt letter is immediately followed by a threesome request, re-establishing him as exactly the disaster Liz diagnosed. The timing and structure are strong: the brief window where Dennis seems redeemable is slammed shut by one word.

jokes.text: Well, you have to admit there's always time for Tony Blair. There's always time for Bashar al-Assad. But there's never any time for Jack Donaghy, and that's a problem.
jokes.setup: Jack is on the phone complaining about his girlfriend's busy schedule.
jokes.punchline: He places himself in competition for time with Tony Blair and Bashar al-Assad — treating his romantic grievance as equivalent to matters of geopolitical importance.
jokes.explanation: Strong Jack character joke — his ego places himself as a peer of world leaders competing for Condi's time. 'There's always time for Bashar al-Assad' is particularly funny because Assad is not someone most people would put in the 'gets meetings' category affectionately. High character integration.

jokes.text: That's why I'm always dating 20-year-olds. / Nah, let me tell you about 20-year-olds, my friend. Half of them are 16.
jokes.setup: Jack explains he dates younger women to avoid the scheduling complications of successful women.
jokes.punchline: Dennis 'helpfully' warns Jack that dating 20-year-olds is risky because half of them are 16 — revealing Dennis's personal experience with this problem.
jokes.explanation: Dark and precise Dennis joke. 'Half of them are 16' — delivered as practical advice from personal experience — is both genuinely disturbing and characteristically Dennis. The dark subversiveness is earned because it fits his established character perfectly. Foreshadows the Dateline reveal.

jokes.text: It's like my cousin Teddy's dog. Sometimes he just doesn't wanna lick my feet. So what I do is, I hide my feet from him for a couple of days, and then when he sees them, he goes bananas. / So Jack, in this example, Liz is the dog. / And I am my feet.
jokes.setup: Dennis offers Jack relationship advice using an extended analogy.
jokes.punchline: The analogy about the dog/feet ends with Dennis clarifying the metaphor — Liz is the dog, he is his own feet — which is both logically airtight and completely insane.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best extended jokes. The dog/feet analogy is already strange (why feet specifically?), but the explicit clarification — 'Liz is the dog, I am my feet' — is a comic delight. Dennis's earnestness in the clarification makes it stranger. The fact that Jack then says 'Yes, I believe I do' (understand) is the final layer: Jack's alpha-male pride allows him to extract genuine advice from Dennis's foot-dog metaphor.

jokes.text: Sensitivity training uh-oh words: slut, ho, bitch, biyatch, queerburger, faggotron, gaybird, the word for black in any language — néro, noir, schwartz, negro, kam-an-sek.
jokes.setup: A sensitivity trainer lists forbidden words for the group.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from common slurs to invented compounds ('queerburger,' 'faggotron,' 'gaybird') to a multilingual survey of the word for 'black.' The made-up words are funnier than the real ones.
jokes.explanation: Strong list comedy with excellent escalation. 'Queerburger,' 'faggotron,' and 'gaybird' are clearly made-up words designed to be so ridiculously specific they could only be deeply offensive to somebody — the joke being that someone clearly used these. The shift to multilingual 'words for black' is a different kind of joke (thoroughness as absurdism). High originality in coinage.

jokes.text: What else can we not call each other? / How about sweaty greaseball? / Ooh, very good. That's highly offensive. / Person of color. / Guess if you say it like that. / Sneaky Taiwanese tranny who stole my watch. / Ho-ho! Yes! These words are terrible.
jokes.setup: The sensitivity training group tries to come up with more offensive terms.
jokes.punchline: The group keeps one-upping itself: 'sweaty greaseball' (ethnic), 'person of color' (technically correct but said wrong), and finally 'sneaky Taiwanese tranny who stole my watch' — which is so specific it implies a real incident.
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'sneaky Taiwanese tranny who stole my watch' is exceptional — the specificity (Taiwanese, tranny, AND theft) implies this is a specific grievance from someone in the room. The trainer's 'Ho-ho! Yes!' acceptance is perfect. 'Person of color / Guess if you say it like that' is an excellent mid-list joke about context.

jokes.text: It's Dr. Martin Luther King, and he did not have a feeling, he had a dream.
jokes.setup: Tracy invokes 'Professor Martin Luther King' and his 'feeling'
jokes.punchline: Toofer corrects both the honorific (Professor vs. Doctor) and the speech ('feeling' vs. 'dream') simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Tracy misquoting MLK in every possible way (wrong title, wrong signature phrase) and Toofer's precise dual correction is a compact, well-structured joke. The correction of 'feeling' to 'dream' is the sharper punchline. Character-perfect for both Tracy and Toofer.

jokes.text: Like professor Martin Luther King said, I have a feeling. / It's Dr. Martin Luther King, and he did not have a feeling, he had a dream.
jokes.setup: Tracy invokes MLK to support his point about racial solidarity.
jokes.punchline: He gets the honorific wrong ('professor') and misquotes the speech ('feeling' instead of 'dream') — Toofer corrects both with barely concealed contempt.
jokes.explanation: A well-built double-error joke — Tracy gets both the title AND the speech wrong, allowing Toofer to correct him twice in one breath. 'He did not have a feeling, he had a dream' is a perfectly dry Toofer line. The double correction structure is neat.

jokes.text: Ah, dude wear khakis. Uncle Tom, party of one.
jokes.setup: Toofer corrects Tracy's MLK misquote with academic precision.
jokes.punchline: Tracy dismisses Toofer's correctness as assimilation ('khakis,' 'Uncle Tom') with a restaurant hostess phrasing ('party of one').
jokes.explanation: 'Uncle Tom, party of one' is a sharp, quotable line that combines the racial accusation with a restaurant seating formality — it's Tracy at his most creative with language. The khakis callback to the earlier 'pants that fit' grievance adds resonance.

jokes.text: You can't call someone that if you've never read the book! / What book?
jokes.setup: Toofer challenges Tracy for calling him 'Uncle Tom.'
jokes.punchline: Tracy has no idea 'Uncle Tom' comes from a book — he thinks it's just an insult name.
jokes.explanation: Clean two-line joke. Tracy's 'What book?' is devastatingly simple — he doesn't know it's from a novel. The economy is excellent: four words reveal everything about the gap between these two characters.

jokes.text: That's it! This is it. This is the sketch we should do. Right here, you and me! This is deep stuff goin' on. We gotta write this. / You're right.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Toofer are in the middle of a genuine, escalating argument about race.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has the show-business instinct to recognize that their real conflict is better content than any pitch — he wants to write their actual argument as a sketch. Toofer immediately agrees.
jokes.explanation: A meta-referential moment: the real conflict becomes art. Tracy's instinct to immediately commodify genuine emotion is a show-business joke and a character joke simultaneously. Toofer's immediate agreement suggests he too sees the opportunity over the hurt. Well-observed.

jokes.text: Liz reads Dennis's pro/con list note: 'I know this might be emotional for you, so there's a meatball sub in the fridge.'
jokes.setup: Liz comes home to find Dennis has left a note, presumably with his goodbye or the pro/con list.
jokes.punchline: The note addresses her emotional state by providing a meatball sub — Dennis's solution to female emotion is carbohydrates.
jokes.explanation: Great Dennis character joke. His emotional intelligence peaks at 'here's a sandwich.' The specificity of 'meatball sub' is better than just 'food' — it's a specific, messy, not-particularly-romantic food. The joke also connects to the earlier thread of Dennis's good moments being food-related.

jokes.text: Liz reads Dennis's pros list. The TV appears mounted on the wall. Cut to: 'Pro. Fixed TV.'
jokes.setup: Liz is writing a pros and cons list about Dennis per Jack's advice
jokes.punchline: The first (apparently only) pro she can identify is 'Fixed TV' — the same TV he was making nine holes in the wall for at the start of the episode
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed visual callback. The mounted TV itself is the punchline — Dennis actually did it, which is simultaneously evidence for and against keeping him. 'Pro. Fixed TV.' as the lone entry on the list says everything about the relationship.

jokes.text: Pro. Fixed TV. (Liz reading Dennis's pro/con list — the visual of a single pro being about the TV)
jokes.setup: Liz is reading Dennis's pro/con list for their relationship.
jokes.punchline: The only 'pro' Liz (or we) get to see is 'Fixed TV' — the wall-mounted hospital TV from the cold open, which was the source of the episode's first conflict.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and visual gag. 'Fixed TV' as the enumerated first pro on the relationship list — after nine holes in the wall and the hospital TV discussion — is a perfect episode callback. It's funny as a structural payoff and as character comedy (Dennis's pro is a thing he did poorly).

jokes.text: Hello, I'm Star Jones. And welcome to the Star Jones Gastric Bypass Cooking Show. / Now you know, I can only eat small portions. / Oh, my goodness! Dessert.
characters: Jenna/Pete in character as Star Jones
jokes.setup: The Tracy/Toofer race relations sketch has been cut; the show is airing the Star Jones cooking show sketch instead.
jokes.punchline: The entire joke of the sketch is Star Jones post-gastric bypass being unable to eat the food on her own cooking show — the irony of a cooking show host who can't eat.
jokes.explanation: Celebrity parody sketch with a clear ironic premise (cooking show host can't eat). 'Now you know, I can only eat small portions' delivered with Star Jones energy is good, though the joke doesn't push much beyond the premise.

jokes.text: Hello, I'm Star Jones. And welcome to the Star Jones Gastric Bypass Cooking Show.
jokes.setup: We're told Tracy replaced the race relations sketch with something else
jokes.punchline: It's a cooking show hosted by Star Jones centered on her gastric bypass surgery — a bizarrely specific celebrity parody
jokes.explanation: The Star Jones Gastric Bypass Cooking Show is a deeply specific, audacious piece of 30 Rock's celebrity satire. The concept itself — a cooking show where the host can only eat tiny portions because of gastric bypass — is a perfect absurd premise with a logical internal consistency. Very much of its cultural moment.

jokes.text: Now you know, I can only eat small portions. / Oh, my goodness! Dessert.
jokes.setup: The Star Jones cooking show continues with its central absurd premise
jokes.punchline: Star Jones can only eat small portions — the entire cooking show premise is that she's surrounded by food she can barely consume
jokes.explanation: The continuation of the sketch. 'Oh, my goodness! Dessert.' is a good reaction beat that plays Star Jones's enthusiasm against her surgical limitations.

jokes.text: Okay, he's right, this is funnier. (Toofer, watching the Star Jones sketch instead of the race relations sketch he championed)
jokes.setup: Toofer had argued passionately for socially conscious comedy over cheap laughs.
jokes.punchline: Watching the Star Jones gastric bypass sketch, he concedes it's funnier than the principled alternative — an admission that undercuts his entire earlier argument.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character button. Toofer's admission that the cheap sketch is funnier is both meta (the show acknowledging it chose entertainment over politics) and a perfect character beat — his principles evaporate when faced with good comedy. High character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Guess where I was last night. / Mark Foley's pajama party. / No. / Kandahar.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz to guess where he was last night.
jokes.punchline: Liz's first guess — 'Mark Foley's pajama party' — is a reference to the then-current Republican Congressional page scandal (Foley had just resigned). Jack's actual answer (Kandahar, Afghanistan) is equally surprising.
jokes.explanation: Sharp contemporary political joke — the Mark Foley reference was extremely timely (Season 1, 2006). Liz's guess as the worse-case scenario from Jack's political world is good character comedy. Kandahar as the actual answer is its own absurd escalation.

jokes.text: Well, I'm glad things are working out for you and your mystery lady. / Well, actually, they're not. I broke up with her. / Really? What happened? / Well, I finally realized that we're not compatible. I mean, I'm all for fantasy role-play, but Abu Ghraib?
jokes.setup: Jack says he and his girlfriend are incompatible because of her fantasy role-play preferences.
jokes.punchline: The fantasy role-play she wanted was Abu Ghraib — the infamous torture prison. Jack's line indicates he's game for many things, but prisoner torture scenarios cross his line.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top-three jokes. The Abu Ghraib role-play as a dealbreaker for Jack Donaghy — a man who flew to Afghanistan to see his girlfriend — is an extraordinary dark comedy choice. The fact that Jack specifies 'I'm all for fantasy role-play, but...' implies his usual tastes are extreme, making Abu Ghraib somehow the line he won't cross. Extremely original, dark, and character-specific. Near-anthology quality.

jokes.text: 'Jack likes Dennis.' / 'Jack likes Dennis.' (Liz writing this repeatedly, apparently in disbelief)
jokes.setup: Jack has said Dennis is 'okay' after bonding over their parallel relationship problems.
jokes.punchline: Liz is apparently so disturbed by Jack's approval of Dennis that she writes it down repeatedly — the visual of Liz processing this impossibility.
jokes.explanation: A good visual reaction beat — Liz writing 'Jack likes Dennis' repeatedly as if trying to make sense of it. The joke is in the cognitive dissonance of Jack Donaghy finding merit in Dennis Duffy. Economical and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: At Snapple, when young fruit ripens, they may want to combine with other fruit.
jokes.setup: An apparently sexual situation is occurring (Liz's apartment, ambiguous context).
jokes.punchline: A Snapple commercial plays whose language — 'young fruit ripens' and 'combine with other fruit' — inadvertently provides sexual commentary on whatever is happening on screen.
jokes.explanation: Meta-visual gag — the Snapple ad's fruit language as sexual double entendre running over a scene. The visual joke requires context we don't have from transcript alone, but the fruit-combining language is clearly a euphemism for what's happening.

jokes.text: It's a fancy briefcase, you know, 'cause you're classy and important. / Like a dude.
jokes.setup: Dennis gives Liz a nice briefcase as a Christmas present, complimenting her as classy and important.
jokes.punchline: 'Like a dude' — he immediately undercuts the compliment by specifying that her importance is male-coded.
jokes.explanation: Economical Dennis joke — he gives a genuine compliment and then immediately undermines it with casual sexism. 'Like a dude' is the perfect two-word punchline. High character integration: this is Dennis trying and failing simultaneously.

jokes.text: I also got you some antihistamine. In case the next guy you're with, you know, has a dog and you wanna stay with him.
jokes.setup: Dennis gives Liz a second gift: antihistamine.
jokes.punchline: The antihistamine is framed as preparation for her future relationships — specifically, so allergies won't prevent her from staying with men who have dogs. Dennis is thoughtfully enabling Liz's dating future without him.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and character joke. Dennis giving Liz antihistamine for 'the next guy with a dog' is simultaneously sweet, sad, and completely Dennis — he's being thoughtful in the most Dennis way possible, simultaneously acknowledging the breakup and helping her replace him. The callback to the Great Dane allergy thread ties the episode together.

jokes.text: I also got you some antihistamine. In case the next guy you're with, you know, has a dog and you wanna stay with him.
jokes.setup: Dennis is saying a final goodbye and wraps up his gifts
jokes.punchline: He's bought Liz antihistamine to help with her next boyfriend's dog — a bizarrely thoughtful, self-erasing gesture
jokes.explanation: A perfect character moment. Dennis gives Liz medication to help her stay with her NEXT boyfriend — simultaneously generous, heartbreaking, and perfectly stupid. The callback to the allergy joke from the episode's opening gives it earned emotional weight. This is Dennis at his most sympathetically realized.

jokes.text: Should I grab a plate? / Yeah. Get me a diet soda.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Liz appear to be reconciling over Chinese food.
jokes.punchline: Liz agrees to share food with Dennis — their reconciliation expressed entirely through dietary logistics — and immediately issues a drink order.
jokes.explanation: A quiet, character-revealing beat — Liz's emotional reconciliation with Dennis is expressed as a food-sharing arrangement and a drink order. Consistent with the 'good moments are food-related' thread. Not a big laugh but a good character note.

jokes.text: Dateline NBC 'To Catch a Predator' cold open plays — Chris Hansen: 'Can I ask you what you're doing here tonight?' / 'Oh, yeah, I'm here to boff some chick named Mary.' / 'Boff some chick—' / 'Oh my God. Do you know how old Mary is?' / 'Yeah, uh, 22. I think.' / 'You wanna try again?' / 'Crap. That girl said she was 16, but I swear to God I could tell she was 22.'
jokes.setup: A Dateline NBC Predator sting segment begins playing; Liz realizes with dawning horror it involves Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Dennis is caught in a Dateline sting, using the word 'boff,' and — most damning — his defense is that he 'could tell she was 22' when she said she was 16.
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural payoff masterpiece. Dennis told Jack that 'half of 20-year-olds are 16' earlier — now it's revealed he has direct personal experience with this. The Dateline segment resolves his earlier warning as autobiography. 'I'm here to boff some chick named Mary' on national television, followed by 'I could tell she was 22' — his defense is that his attraction to her means she seemed older. Perfect callback, devastating escalation, complete character payoff. One of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: Yeah, uh, 22. I think. / You wanna try again? / Crap. / That girl said she was 16, but I swear to God I could tell she was 22.
jokes.setup: Chris Hansen asks Dennis how old he thought the girl was
jokes.punchline: Dennis's self-correction reveals the girl was actually 16 — and his defense ('I could tell she was 22') is a perfect inversion of the usual predator logic
jokes.explanation: Dennis's defense — 'she said she was 16, but I swear I could tell she was 22' — is the exact logical inversion of a predator's usual claim, and it makes the situation much worse while somehow seeming like he thinks it helps. The callback to his earlier 'half of them are 16' wisdom is devastating.

jokes.text: Get out of my apartment! / This happened while we were broken up. / No, no, no, no. I was right about you! / This is a con, by the way. You on Dateline is a con!
jokes.setup: Liz sees Dennis on Dateline and kicks him out.
jokes.punchline: Dennis insists (1) the timing matters (during the breakup), and (2) Dateline itself is a con — he's the real victim of a sting operation.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's counter-argument — that Dateline is the real con — is perfectly in character. His belief that being caught in a predator sting is a journalistic trick rather than evidence of predatory behavior is both funny and horrifying. 'This happened while we were broken up' is a great additional defense that only Dennis would deploy.

jokes.text: You know what? I knew you wouldn't be cool about this. / We're finished. / You can't break up with me. I already broke up with you! / Fine! / Then we agree to disagree!
jokes.setup: Liz tries to break up with Dennis after the Dateline revelation.
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims she can't break up with him because he already broke up with her (from the letter), leading to a mutual-breakup standoff resolved by 'we agree to disagree' — as if a breakup is a matter of opinion.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant episode-closer joke. 'You can't break up with me, I already broke up with you' is structurally perfect — it callbacks to Dennis's letter while adding a new dimension of absurd proprietary control over the breakup. 'We agree to disagree' as the resolution to a breakup is a perfect final Dennis line — treating an emotional rupture as a negotiating impasse. High quotability and strong callbacks to the squatter's rights joke that opened the episode.

tmdb_overview: When Liz finally dumps her boyfriend Dennis, she prowls the singles scene under Jenna's tutelage. Love also stinks for Jack, as he discovers dating a Bush administration official has its downside. And Tracy and Toofer clash, which lands both in sensitivity training.
insight: Absurdist character comedy sustains 60 jokes across Season 1's densest episode.
